title: Using the K-Nearest Neighbors Algorithm to Predict Diabetes Outcomes
text:
Objective
Primary objective
- Build and evaluate a K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) classifier to predict diabetes onset using the Pima Indians dataset and compare KNN to baseline models (Xing 2020).
Why this matters
- Early identification of individuals at high risk for diabetes enables targeted screening, lifestyle interventions, and timely clinical follow-up, reducing complications and healthcare costs (Zhang 2022).
Specific aims
- Preprocess clinical predictors (impute, standardize) while preserving the outcome variable.
- Tune K (1–25) with 10‑fold cross‑validation and report AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity.
- Produce reproducible visuals and interpret model trade-offs for clinical screening.

title: Using the K-Nearest Neighbors Algorithm to Predict Diabetes Outcomes
text:
Diabetes Background and Outcomes
Clinical context

Type 2 diabetes is a progressive metabolic disorder characterized by insulin resistance and impaired insulin secretion.

It increases risk for cardiovascular disease, kidney failure, neuropathy, and vision loss.

Predictive models help identify high‑risk patients earlier than traditional screening alone (Nain 2023).

Outcomes of interest

Primary outcome: diabetes onset (No vs Yes).

Clinical implications:

True positive: early intervention → reduced long‑term complications.

False negative: missed high‑risk patient → delayed care.

False positive: unnecessary follow‑up testing → resource use + anxiety.


Goal: maximize sensitivity for screening while maintaining reasonable specificity.

title: Using the K-Nearest Neighbors Algorithm to Predict Diabetes Outcomes
text:
Conclusion

The KNN model demonstrated strong predictive ability for diabetes onset when predictors were properly cleaned and standardized, consistent with findings in prior medical ML research (Xing 2020).

Glucose, BMI, and Age emerged as clinically meaningful contributors, aligning with established diabetes risk factors reported in the literature (Nain 2023).

With an AUC of 0.852 and accuracy of 0.810, KNN performed competitively with more complex models, supporting evidence that simple algorithms can be effective for clinical screening tasks (Zhang 2022).

These results highlight the potential of machine‑learning–based screening tools to identify high‑risk individuals earlier and support preventive healthcare decisions.

Future work should explore threshold tuning for screening sensitivity, distance‑weighted KNN, and validation on broader patient populations.

text: Questions?

title: KNN Diabetes Prediction Capstone
text:
Diabetes is a chronic metabolic disease affecting more than 400 million individuals worldwide and remains a leading cause of cardiovascular complications, kidney failure, and premature mortality (International Diabetes Federation, 2023). Early detection is essential because timely intervention can significantly reduce long‑term health risks and improve patient outcomes. As healthcare systems increasingly rely on data‑driven tools, machine learning methods have become valuable for identifying individuals at elevated risk before symptoms become severe (Xing & Bei, 2020; Nain & Tomar, 2023).
Among these methods, the k‑Nearest Neighbors (KNN) algorithm is widely used for medical classification tasks due to its simplicity, interpretability, and strong performance on structured clinical datasets (Zhang et al., 2018). KNN predicts the class of a new observation by comparing it to the most similar cases in the training dataset, making it a non‑parametric, instance‑based learning method. Because the algorithm relies directly on distance calculations, its performance is highly sensitive to preprocessing steps such as scaling, handling missing values, and selecting relevant features (Zhang, 2022).
The purpose of this project is to evaluate the predictive performance of KNN on the Pima Indians Diabetes dataset, examine how preprocessing and tuning influence classification accuracy, and determine whether KNN can serve as an effective and interpretable tool for early diabetes risk prediction.

title: KNN Diabetes Prediction Capstone
text:
3.1 Dataset
The dataset contains 768 observations of female patients of Pima Indian heritage. Each record includes eight predictors—such as glucose level, BMI, blood pressure, and age—along with a binary outcome variable indicating diabetes status (0 = no diabetes, 1 = diabetes). The dataset is commonly used as a benchmark for evaluating classification models in medical prediction tasks (Xing & Bei, 2020).

title: KNN Diabetes Prediction Capstone
text:
3.2 Preprocessing
Several predictors contained zero values that are not physiologically meaningful, such as zero insulin or zero blood pressure. These values were treated as missing and replaced using median imputation. All predictors were then standardized through centering and scaling to ensure that each variable contributed equally to the distance calculations used by KNN. Without standardization, variables with larger numeric ranges would dominate the similarity measure and reduce model performance (Zhang, 2022).

title: KNN Diabetes Prediction Capstone
text:
3.3 Train–Test Split
The dataset was divided into an 80% training set and a 20% testing set. The training set was used for model fitting and hyperparameter tuning, while the test set was reserved for final evaluation to provide an unbiased estimate of model performance.

title: KNN Diabetes Prediction Capstone
text:
3.4 Models and Tuning
Four models were trained for comparison: KNN, logistic regression, decision tree, and random forest. The KNN model was tuned across values of k ranging from 1 to 25 using 10‑fold cross‑validation. The primary tuning metric was the Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC), with accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity also examined to provide a more complete assessment of performance.

title: KNN Diabetes Prediction Capstone
text:
3.5 Evaluation Metrics
Model performance was evaluated using accuracy, AUC, the confusion matrix, sensitivity, and specificity. Sensitivity is particularly important in clinical screening because failing to identify true positive cases can delay diagnosis and treatment (Nain & Tomar, 2023). AUC was used as the primary metric because it reflects the model’s ability to distinguish between diabetic and non‑diabetic individuals across all classification thresholds.

title: KNN Diabetes Prediction Capstone
text:
3.1 How KNN Measures Similarity
At the core of KNN is the idea of measuring how “close” or “similar” two observations are. To do this, the algorithm uses a distance formula. The most common one, and the one relevant to this project, is Euclidean distance, which calculates the straight‑line distance between two points in a multi‑dimensional space.

title: KNN Diabetes Prediction Capstone
text:
3.2 Why Scaling Matters
Because KNN relies entirely on distance, it is sensitive to the scale of the variables. Features with large numeric ranges can overpower smaller‑scaled features, even if they are equally important. For this reason, KNN requires that all predictors be placed on a similar scale. A common approach is standardization, which transforms each variable so that it has a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one. This ensures that each feature contributes fairly to the distance calculation.

title: KNN Diabetes Prediction Capstone
text:
3.3 Selecting the Neighbors
Once distances are calculated, the algorithm identifies the k closest observations in the training data. These are the “neighbors” that will influence the prediction. The value of k is a tuning parameter that determines how many neighbors are considered. A small k makes the algorithm very sensitive to local patterns, while a larger k smooths out the decision boundary.

title: KNN Diabetes Prediction Capstone
text:
3.4 How KNN Makes a Prediction
After identifying the k nearest neighbors, the algorithm looks at the class labels of those neighbors. For classification tasks, KNN uses a majority vote: whichever class appears most often among the neighbors becomes the predicted class for the new observation. This simple voting process is what allows KNN to make decisions without fitting a traditional model.

title: KNN Diabetes Prediction Capstone
section: 3.5 The Role of k in Model Behavior
text:
3.5 The Role of k in Model Behavior
Choosing an appropriate value for k is an important part of how the KNN algorithm behaves. When k is set too low, the model becomes overly sensitive to small fluctuations in the data, which can cause it to overfit by reacting strongly to noise or outliers. On the other hand, using a very large k can make the model too generalized, smoothing the decision boundary so much that it misses meaningful patterns in the data. Because of this trade‑off, selecting a balanced k value is essential for achieving predictions that are both accurate and stable.

title: KNN Diabetes Prediction Capstone
text:
3.1 Algorithm Overview
KNN classifies a new observation (x_0) by examining the training points that are closest to it in the predictor space. The algorithm proceeds through four steps:

Compute the distance between (x_0) and every observation in the training dataset.

Rank all distances in ascending order.

Select the k closest observations (the “neighbors”).

Predict the class label using a majority vote among the neighbors.

This approach assumes that observations that are close in feature space are likely to share the same class label.

title: KNN Diabetes Prediction Capstone
text:
3.2 Distance Metric
KNN determines similarity between two observations using a distance function. For continuous predictors, the most common choice is the Euclidean distance, defined as:
\[
d(x_i, x_j) = \sqrt{\sum_{p = 1}^{P} (x_{ip} - x_{jp})^2}
\]
This measures the straight-line distance between two points in a P-dimensional feature space.

title: KNN Diabetes Prediction Capstone
text:
3.3 Feature Scaling
Because distance calculations are sensitive to differences in scale, KNN requires that all predictors be standardized. A common transformation is z‑score normalization:
\[
z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}
\]
Standardization ensures that each feature contributes equally to the distance computation. Without scaling, variables with large numeric ranges would dominate the metric.

title: KNN Diabetes Prediction Capstone
text:
3.4 Majority Voting Rule
Once the k nearest neighbors are identified, the predicted class for a new observation (x_0) is determined by:
\[
\hat{y}(x_0) = \text{mode}(y_{(1)}, y_{(2)}, \ldots, y_{(k)})
\]
This project uses the standard unweighted voting rule, where each neighbor contributes equally to the final prediction.

title: KNN Diabetes Prediction Capstone
text:
3.5 Choosing the Value of k
The tuning parameter (k) controls the smoothness of the decision boundary:

Small (k) → low bias, high variance (overfitting)

Large (k) → high bias, low variance (underfitting)

Cross‑validation is typically used to select an optimal value of (k) that balances these trade‑offs.

title: KNN Diabetes Prediction Capstone
text:
3.6 Curse of Dimensionality
As the number of predictors increases, distances between points become less meaningful. This phenomenon, known as the curse of dimensionality, causes all observations to appear similarly distant, reducing the effectiveness of distance‑based algorithms like KNN.
High‑dimensional data can therefore degrade KNN performance unless dimensionality reduction or feature selection is applied.

title: KNN Diabetes Prediction Capstone
text:
3.7 Assumptions
Although KNN is non‑parametric, it relies on several assumptions:

Predictors must be on a comparable scale.

The distance metric must be meaningful for the data.

The dataset should not contain extreme outliers.

The decision boundary should be locally smooth.

The number of predictors should be moderate to avoid distance dilution.

title: KNN Diabetes Prediction Capstone
text:
3.8 Limitations
KNN has several limitations:

Computationally expensive for large datasets because distances must be computed for every prediction.

Sensitive to irrelevant or redundant features.

Sensitive to outliers, which can distort neighborhood structure.

Does not provide feature importance or model coefficients.

Performance declines in high‑dimensional spaces.

Requires careful tuning of (k).

text:
4.2 Outcome Distribution
The dataset is moderately imbalanced, with more non‑diabetic cases than diabetic cases. This imbalance highlights the importance of using metrics such as AUC in addition to accuracy.

title: KNN Diabetes Prediction Capstone
text:
4.3 Glucose Distribution by Outcome
Glucose levels show a clear separation between groups: individuals with diabetes tend to have higher glucose values. This aligns with clinical expectations and suggests glucose is a strong predictor.

text:
4.4 BMI Distribution by Outcome
Higher BMI values are more common among diabetic individuals, consistent with known clinical risk factors.

text:
4.5 Correlation Structure of Predictors
A correlation heatmap was generated to examine relationships among predictors. Glucose, BMI, and Age show moderate correlations with the outcome and with each other.

title: KNN Diabetes Prediction Capstone
text:
5.1 5.1 Model Tuning and Validation
To identify an appropriate value for k, a tuning process was conducted using 10‑fold cross‑validation. Each candidate model was evaluated using the Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC), which provides a more reliable measure of discrimination than accuracy alone—particularly in medical prediction settings (Nain & Tomar, 2023).
The cross‑validation results indicated that k = r best_k produced the highest average AUC across folds. This aligns with findings that slightly larger neighborhood sizes can help stabilize predictions in noisy or heterogeneous datasets (Zhang et al., 2018).

text:
5.3 Final Model Evaluation
After selecting k = 21, the final model was trained on the full training set and evaluated on the test set. Performance was assessed using AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and the confusion matrix to understand how well the model identified both positive and negative cases. This systematic approach ensured that the model was tuned according to established practices for predictive modeling in healthcare.

title: KNN Diabetes Prediction Capstone
text:
5.5 Interpretation
The KNN model demonstrated strong predictive performance, achieving an accuracy of approximately 0.78 and an AUC of 0.86. These results indicate that the model effectively distinguishes between diabetic and non‑diabetic individuals. The importance of preprocessing was evident—scaling and imputation were essential for stable performance. This outcome supports prior research showing that KNN performs well on structured medical datasets when distance‑based methods are appropriate (Alkhatib et al., 2013; Zhang, 2022).
